newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian gilts end higher on low call money rates.
newsitem.headline: Indian gilts end higher on low call money rates.

text.p: Low call money rates led to increased trade in Indian government securities and pushed up prices on Wednesday, dealers said.
They said call money ended the day at 1.0-1.25 percent, down from opening quotes of 5.0-5.75 percent.
"The supply of funds is far in excess of demand at the moment," said a dealer. "Besides recent dollar purchases by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has also added to domestic liquidity."
The RBI has been buying dollars in recent months to arrest the rise of the rupee. Dollar purchases by the central bank inject rupees into the banking system.
Dealers said prices of government securities moved up sharply on increased buying interest. They said Wednesday's trades were worth 3.28 billion rupees against the previous 2.46.

"Prices went up across all maturities today," said a dealer at a private bank. "There is a feeling that call rates will remain easy for the next couple of months unless the government borrowings programme starts."
He said it was not clear if there would be any market borrowings in the immediate future, given the uncertain political climate.
"Of course, the ways and means advances will be there..but form banks' point of view, there will be no outflows unless a loan issue is there," he said.
The 13.50 percent 1997 stock traded on Wednesday at 101.62 rupees against its last traded 101.53 and the 13.50 percent 1998 at 103.42 against 103.20.

Other securities which registered a sharp increase in prices included the 13.82 percent 2002 which rose to 102.55 rupees from 102.10, the 13.40 percent 1999 which appreciated to 102.67 from 102.40 and the 13.70 percent 1999 which rose to 103.30 from 103.13, dealers said.
Treasury bills maturing in July yielded 9.15 percent while August bills yielded 9.30 percent.
